verdict.tagline: Endless procedural stars and deep base building, weathered by technical friction.
for_you_if: you want endless procedural worlds to explore and build across
you enjoy gathering resources and upgrading equipment over long campaigns
you appreciate regular content updates without microtransactions
not_for_you_if: you expect a fast tutorial without heavy resource grinding
you need stable frame rates and seamless multiplayer without bugs
you are bothered by repetitive mission structures over time

Total: 0/10, remarkably terrible. Graphics: 4/10, OK, but not great, cartoonish. Story: Not that kind of game. Gameplay; 4/10, simplistic scavenging and crafting akin to Minecraft. Was still stuck in a needlessly long and boring tutorial after 100 minutes: -1 to total score. There are constantly an enormous amount of text and other HUD-items cluttering the screen, yet a handful of tutorial steps remain so poorly explained that I had to consult Google: -1 to total score. Experienced two severe glitches so far; A. couldn't answer incoming transmission, pressing "X" did nothing, had to restart game, B. couldn't fit more than 10 Carbon in inventory, even after moving everything else to ship: -2 to total score.

I feel very conflicted about this game. It is extremely large, has a relatively small file size, runs well, but the main gameplay aspect is extremely grindy. If you are into games where you spend hours finding resources to repair your deprecated tools, this is 100% the game for you. Overall though, it's a decent game that you should try at least once to see if you like it.

I wanted to like this game, but it wasn't for me.

My first impression was that the tutorial dragged on far too long. Nearly 80 minutes into the game, I was still being sent on resource-gathering errands and building a base instead of feeling like I was exploring the universe. A poor starting planet didn't help, as much of my time was spent walking around looking for basic materials rather than doing anything exciting.

The controls and camera also felt awkward to me, and I never reached a point where movement or exploration felt comfortable. While I understand the game opens up later, I don't think a player should have to spend several hours waiting for the fun to begin.

Not a bad game—just one whose opening hours failed to hook me.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the gameplay loop as heavily focused on continuous gathering, crafting, and refilling resources like oxygen, fuel, and hazard protection.

citations.review_text: People behind this have no freaking clue what game design is. The whole gameplay loop is gathering crap @ fixing broken crap @ refilling crap @ repeat. Pointless scavenging with no interesting encounters, mechanics or basically anything that I can consider worthy of time.

The core gameplay is FINE if you are really into that: exploration. But don't expect depth in any of the other content the game offers, it is all extremely shallow and serves only as dressing for the main "thing" of the game.

The biggest issue, BY FAR, of this game, is the baffling design choices that you encounter constantly. Things that make you tab out and google to make sure you're not stupid and just missing something, just to find out that no, it's by design, and people have been complaining about it since the game's release.
Some quick ones that are noticeable within 30 minutes of playing; 
No "save and quit", you have to find a save point, or enter/leave your ship, and then alt-f4 as your only means of leaving the game.

The tutorial tells you to go somewhere, and puts a visible marker for you to go to. The marker however then dissapears, and the tool you can build to locate things, such as that marker you need to find, is not unlocked yet, so you better have remembered!

Speaking of the tutorial, you get a little text box at the bottom of your screen that tells you the next steps that you have to work for, which is nice. HOWEVER, this box constantly switches from the objective you're on (eg: "craft a wire to repair the ship"), to useless text akin to "mine iron ore for iron :)", and the only way to get the useful guide/objective back up is to wait for the chaff to cycle through, like an ad.

Pressing escape will, unintuitively, not close whatever menu you're inside of; it will open a separate compendium-style menu. This means that constantly while playing you will be opening and closing 3-5 different menus by accident for something that should have taken one key press.

Some quests require you to craft things to repair machines/etc, but they won't just let you craft it in your inventory, where the thing you need to repair is; you have to switch to another tab in your inventory, craft the component you need (hope you remembered what it was!), an…

No Man’s Sky is one of those games that I really wanted to love more than I actually loved playing.

The atmosphere and sense of scale are genuinely impressive at first. Landing on new planets, flying into space seamlessly, and discovering strange creatures creates a strong initial feeling of wonder. But after several hours, I realized the core gameplay loop just wasn’t engaging enough for me.  Also, the creatures and planets all started to feel the same very quickly.

Most of my time felt spent:

mining resources
refueling systems
crafting materials
scanning things
flying to another marker
repeating the same cycle

For me, the game felt more wide than deep. The exploration started to lose its magic once I realized most interactions boiled down to variations of the same tasks with no real goal.

I also found the progression lacking tension or meaningful stakes. There wasn’t much unpredictability, danger, or emergent gameplay pushing me to adapt creatively. It felt more like a chill resource-management/exploration game than an actual survival adventure.  However the exploration didn't feel unique either.

If you’re looking for:

high tension
meaningful survival pressure
dynamic encounters
strategic depth
memorable emergent moments

this may not click for you the way it didn’t for me.

I was hoping this would be a fun survival/crafting game, but it was very disappointing.

This game is actually one of the most overrated pieces of garbage I’ve ever wasted money and time on. People kept hyping it up like it was some limitless universe exploration masterpiece, but after a few hours you realize the entire game loop is just mining rocks, refilling oxygen, refilling fuel, refilling life support, and staring at procedurally generated planets that all feel the exact same with different color filters slapped on top.

“No Man’s Sky” should honestly be renamed to “No Man’s Fun.”

Every planet is:

* land on planet
* scan 3 ugly animals
* collect ferrite dust for the 900th time
* repair some broken garbage
* fly to another empty planet
* repeat forever until your brain melts

The exploration is fake depth. There are billions of planets but somehow all of them feel soulless. After the first 10 planets you’ve basically seen the entire game already. Wow, another toxic wasteland with weird broccoli-looking creatures walking around. Incredible innovation.

And the inventory management is absolutely miserable. Half the gameplay is just cleaning your backpack like you’re working in a cosmic warehouse simulator instead of exploring space. Every five minutes:
“Inventory full.”
“Technology damaged.”
“Not enough fuel.”
“Hazard protection falling.”

SHUT UP.

The combat is terrible, the gunplay feels like shooting plastic toys, space battles are stiff and repetitive, and enemy AI has the intelligence of a dying toaster. Even pirates somehow manage to make space combat feel boring.

And don’t even get me started on multiplayer. The universe is supposedly infinite yet somehow everything still feels empty and lifeless. Playing with friends just turns the grind into co-op suffering. “Bro come help me farm carbon for 40 minutes so we can build another ugly metal box base on a planet nobody cares about.”

People defend this game because of the updates, but adding 500 updates to a boring core game is like putting glitter on a trash bag. Sure, there’s “more content”…

citations.review_text: Very fun. I love the open world environment, and the fact that the entire world is procedurally generated leading to infinite possibilities of planets to discover is absolutely brilliant. 10/10

I have about 55 hours on this game on the Xbox version from my friends gamepass, was so good that I bought it on steam lol, this game has quite a lot, it uses procedural generation for all the planets, and it mixes and matches basically every ship, mineral, flora, and fauna, you can find, besides a few locked things like hazardous plants and other small stuff, this game apparently has around ~18 quintillion planets, which is obviously a LOT, now because there are so many planets, you're bound to run into some that are extremely similar, same thing with the fora and fauna, which is honestly completely fine, because I am suprised enough at how many different things they even made in the first place, the decorations and base building parts are also abundent, which I did not expect at first, you can also make your own ship with the right parts, and get pets, which is very enjoyable. This game is definitly gonna be one of my favorites, alongside stuff like Satisfactory, and Sea Of Thieves! [The game also runs pretty good with what I got, some planets and area do have some bad frames or frame drop, but the lowest lows are around 40-70 and the highest highs being 75-130, which really isn't that bad for everything this game has to offer!]

citations.review_text: HIGHLY recommend this game. It is a bit boring during the first little bit of it but once you actually get into the game and start seeing everything that it has to offer, it is a lot of fun, especially with your friends. When you start getting into building your own ships (corvettes and stuff like that) it is a bit tedious even if you are following a guide but other than that building stuff like ships is really fun if you're a creative type of person. 9/10 game right here.

I heard about No Man's Sky when it first came out and how disappointed people were by the launch so I held off buying it. Fast forward 10 years later, I got a random YouTube video in my recommended talking about how much it improved over the years and how the devs continuously push out updates. Being curious, I checked the steam page and decided to give it a shot and honestly? This has got to be the best space game I've ever played. It starts out slow where you wake up on a planet alone, and have to repair a crashed ship. You then gain access to more and more materials, an economy, lots of quests / storyline, ship building, base building, automation - basically everything and more. Every time I boot this game up I run into something new - just as I think I've seen all of the mechanics and features. 10/10 would recommend. The devs deserve massive kudos for this one.

To anyone who's curious: I'm playing on linux and have had no issue with proton compatibility / lag / bugs

I played no man's sky on release day on ps4. I played it for longer than most people should. I loved my time with it... i'm a big ol sci fi fan so its not hard for a space game to grab my attention. 

I'm going to recommend this game to people that haven't played it like me, cause you don't know. 

Now here is my critique... The first SEVERAL hours of this game are LITERALLY unchanged from its initial release. Nothing feels different, you are mining grabbing stuff, and just spend your first few hours doing the same things you did ON DAY 1 with a few extra steps and things you need to upgrade. Which for me? was extremely off putting... 

Then I got into the settlement stuff, started having fun with that, and then you have to wait 20/40/50/2 hours to complete a building. I'm sure the intent is for you to do things in the mean time, but I don't like it. Why can't i upgrade multiple buildings? its not like it takes citizens to upgrade them? if it did i would prioritize getting citizens but it doesn't... So why can't i upgrade multiple things at once?

this is the part where i realized this game is okay with wasting your time. I jumped on to upgrade a building that would take 2 hours to finish upgrading. I then went to work out, and make food, and came back to realize what i had always feared but i had just forgotten to do. If you don't jump into your ship and jump out to save that EXTREMELY important interaction/upgrade. Guess what? it never happened. I'm at the point in time in my life where I dont like games that waste my time, or have mechanics where i have to wait, especially if it doesn't make sense. 

why can't i upgrade my overseer building and the more i upgrade that the more upgrades i can have active at a single time?

why can't i see the materials i need so i can go gather them while its upgrading? it just says "you have an active upgrade happening on another building" come on bro... that's just cheeks. 

maybe its totally my fault and I should haven't messed…
Good game. first 3h to 10h is kinda boring but after it gets great

claims.claim: Reviewers state that default survival mechanics offer virtually no real risk of death.

citations.review_text:
I remember years ago when this game initially released a review along the lines of "Wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle". So I stayed away. I at some point but this game back on my wishlist since the overall sentiment online appears to be praise for the devs for supporting the game and making it much better and more fleshed out. Even the steam page is still 91% positive at time of writing. Finally decided to pick it up. I genuinely cannot fathom how shallow the game used to be if this is the better version, because that review I half remember from years ago is still 100% true. The game is so vast, but so very shallow.

I've got over 80 hours entirely in the last 2 weeks. The core of waking up on a planet get a ship to explore and survive is cool. I want to find out why I'm here and the game explicitly makes you question what you are and why you are doing anything. Not a unique idea but the way it's presented is quite entertaining... until you start to see how little game there actually is here. To call it survival crafting is a misnomer, because at default settings you are at 0 risk of death in 99% of circumstances. In 80 hours I died once and that was from attacking a group of giant mechs with a mining laser then standing there getting shot trying to switch to my gun. It's a crafting game with survival mechanics that mean nothing. And damn does this game LOVE crafting. So much of your time in the game is resource collecting and inventory management. And it has the cardinal sin of [b]NOT BEING ABLE TO CRAFT [i]IN YOUR INVENTORY WITH MATS FROM STORAGE 10 FEET AWAY[/i]. HOW DOES EVERY GAME KEEP ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ THAT UP.[/b] *ahem* There is also a space-trucker trading economy hiding in the extremely boring cookie cutter space stations. Base building. Make money, buy personal ships, buy capital ships, build a fleet, customize to your hearts content. That's not a bad thing, in fact it's the best part of the experience. But the game wants you to think there is a reason, a WHY. And…

Awesome graphics, awesome gameplay, fine optimisation, and a ton of content. It may seem as walking simulator, or  too much grind, but it's less than 5% of the game. The longer you play, the less you need to walk or grind for materials, so it doesn't get repetetive as some might say. Would reccomend if you like exploration and calm gameplay. However, the game offers survival and permadeath mode (or even custom difficulty), which allows for much more challenging gameplay than usually.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that missions and exploration become repetitive, featuring similar structures and recycled content across planets.

citations.review_text:
The biggest issue is that many of the main missions feel like extended tutorials rather than meaningful story progression. A lot of my time was spent traveling back and forth between planets, stations, and NPCs instead of experiencing exciting gameplay. The constant travel eventually became repetitive.

The final Atlas mission was especially disappointing. After completing such an important objective, having my ship and multitool completely damaged felt more like a punishment than a reward. Instead of feeling satisfied after finishing a major storyline, I was given another repair grind. That completely killed the sense of achievement for me.

I understand this may fit the game's design philosophy, where the journey never truly ends, but players who enjoy games with clear progression and rewarding conclusions may find this frustrating.

What I loved:

Beautiful universe and atmosphere.
Excellent base-building system.
Great freedom to explore.
Amazing visual updates over the years.

What I didn't enjoy:

Main missions often feel like long tutorials.
Too much repetitive travel between objectives.
Story progression feels slow.
The ending of the Atlas path doesn't feel rewarding.
Damaging the player's equipment after a major milestone discourages rather than motivates.

Overall, I respect the incredible work and dedication the developers have put into No Man's Sky over the years. It's simply not the type of progression-focused experience I personally enjoy. I may return in the future if friends want to play together, but as a solo player, I was hoping for a more satisfying sense of accomplishment after completing the main storyline.

its annoying, the game always crash during hyperdrive to other system (because of too much animation, when they could just simplify that loading screen into a static one as an option). It also has several bugs in some mission quests, where they don't complete and had to restart. Once you are warped in a new area, some objects take too long to load, especially on settlement, anomaly, and freighter, the walls and floor are missing, and takes about a minute or two to load the surroundings. Plus the missions are too repetitive that it becomes frustrating especially the "Base Computer Archives" also "Deep Ocean" (you go back and forth with base terminals which feels like a grind, no story but just a log text that you read from the terminal) and "Agricultural Research" (going back and forth from planet base to freighter ship farmer just to plant every species, why not just plant them all together and harvest all at once but no, the developers make you grind those repetitive waypoints). The developers lack creativity in story so they just make you grind going from point A to point B, then to top all your worse experience, the game crash during hyperdrive to another system. So overall, for a game that has been launched since 2016, it does feel like the game is still in beta phase when it should already be fun and engaging to play. Wish it had more better story or maybe adding a family system/ love interest into it. There is no gender selection for your player.

We all know the story of no man's sky at this point. I have real respect to the devs for continuing to put out new updates to this game year after year. Never once have they charged me for a dlc, battle pass, or some kind of cosmetic. Despite all this i dont really know if i can recommend no man's sky. 

as a teen i had put nearly 200 hours into this game and since then roughly 30 or so more when i come by to see whatever expansion catches my eye. its a game i want to like. its just really, really, really boring. looking at it now i can imagine that the first time you play it this game is really cool. theres lots of things to do, lots of things to see, but as you go around doing and seeing these thing they all start to blend together. youve seen one tropical planet youve seen them all. exploration on the whole is a bust, its the same buildings everywhere with a different coat of paint, the same sentinels, the same repeatable quests. 
the expeditions serve as a temporary distraction from this sameness, a nice little questline that shows you the in and out of a new update. my only real issue with them is that they are timegated. but even they dont solve the core issue. once you know how to easily get a good weapon, how to easily get currency, how to easily get a good ship then even the expeditions fall apart and your forced to look at what gameplay these tools exist in service of. 
grounded combat is bad, the camera is far to interested in the back of the players head and first person is quite ugly somehow. the sentinels pose no real threat to the player incredibly quickly, becoming more of a increasingly ignorable annoyance and a occasional good source of nanites. the small dissident sentinels have had a issue where their drops spawn to low to the ground and fall out of bounds for as long as i can remember them in the game. 
space combat is somehow worse. the game likes to have big showpiece fights in space, the raider dreadnaught for example, but the combat in those…

The game is perfect for grinders and pure explorers. The planets are beautiful and their ecosystems very well-designed and full of life. The aliens and their technologies also have unique design to them, as well as ships, portals, etc. The corvette is fully customizable, and the personalization doesn't stop there, there is still base building and frigate, which is a lot larger in scale and many other amenities.

However, as much as I like how the devs redeem this game over quite a long time, I gotta say the game fell short just after a while for me. First thing: lack of QoL. Things like the jetpack jump interfering with normal jump and weapon operation really ruin my combat and ore mining experience. Climbing the ladder feels like eternity and the character just auto-climb whenver near it, like in trade outposts, and this is very annoying. Accessing storage is just a hassle, and without essential ores to build a camp and claim the base it's gonna take a while to dump all the stuff into other inventories (also they do not have auto-sorting in storage). There are many more, and I feel like the game this old should have already addressed these things. Second thing: things feel flat and repetitive after a while. Sure there are a lot of things that you can do when visiting a new system, meeting aliens there, setting up camps, etc. Space combat gets boring after a few hours for me, which I think should be a main focus of a game with space as the center of its attraction. Quantity cannot beat quality, and this inevitably comes sooner or later (later for me). 

The game has its own charm, and with me those 97 hours were definitely worth it. But it would not be something that I can binge anymore. And I just wanna specify a few things for other people who just wander into this exquisitely-built but poorly-optimized jack-of-all-trade game. If you want to explore the galaxies and chill while watching two sunsets, then this is for you. But if you also want other flavors of t…

claims.claim: Reviewers highlight seamless transitions when flying from space directly onto planetary surfaces without loading screens.

citations.review_text:
Once upon a time, I was convinced I would never play this game. 10 years after release, I finally decide to give it a shot.

It's good, y'all. It's really good. 

I was just entertained, until I built my first Corvette; that's when I fell in love with the game. Suddenly, I really felt like I was living the fantasy of wandering the universe. Knowing there's still so much to do and explore is wild.

PROS
It is very satisfying, visually. Seeing the biome of a new planet still floors me, each and every time. I get very excited doing my initial scans of the flora and fauna. The process of entering and exiting atmospheres, as well as warping from system to system really fulfills all my immersion needs.
The most important positive is the depth of the game. This many hours in, and I still feel like I've only scratched the surface of what's possible. 

CONS
I will say, it does feel empty. If you're looking for social immersion or a feeling of role play from the NPCs, NMS will probably disappoint you. Planets are somehow diverse and samey. Biomes are gorgeous, but somehow all contain the same resources, collected with the same methods, each and every time.

Recommended!! 10/10.

If you told me back in 2016 that No Man’s Sky would become the gold standard for space exploration, I would have laughed. But Hello Games actually did the impossible. Here is why this game is an absolute masterpiece today:

The Incredible Seamlessness:
Flying from outer space, through the atmosphere, and landing right on a planet’s surface with absolutely zero loading screens is still legendary. Being able to just hop into your ship and travel between multiple planets in a massive star system without a single pause is an unmatched level of immersion. It never gets old.

The Constant Free Updates:
The dedication here is unreal. Every single year, the devs drop massive, game-changing updates for free. They don’t just add small items; they completely overhaul core mechanics, expand the lore, and add entire new gameplay loops. Half the time, the game gets improved so much that it's barely recognizable from the year before.

The Ultimate Comeback:
We all know NMS had a notoriously terrible launch. But instead of taking the money and running, the team put their heads down and worked. They turned a total disaster into the most influential and best game in the space exploration genre. It remains incredibly relevant today and still pulls in massive success, which is mind-blowing considering they don't monetize existing players at all. No paid DLCs, no battle passes, no microtransactions, just pure love for the game.

This wasn't even all of it but if I would mention everything that makes this game amazing, we would be here for another day

If you love space, exploration, or just want to support one of the consumer-friendliest dev teams in gaming history, buy this. You won't regret it.

What keeps pulling me back is the atmosphere and sense of discovery. Flying seamlessly from orbit to planet surface still hits every time, and the game constantly rewards curiosity instead of forcing a checklist. It’s one of the few games where I can genuinely relax, explore, build, survive, or just disappear into the universe for a few hours.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the main missions and quests as repetitive grinds that require traveling back and forth between waypoints and terminals.

citations.review_text:
The biggest issue is that many of the main missions feel like extended tutorials rather than meaningful story progression. A lot of my time was spent traveling back and forth between planets, stations, and NPCs instead of experiencing exciting gameplay. The constant travel eventually became repetitive.

The final Atlas mission was especially disappointing. After completing such an important objective, having my ship and multitool completely damaged felt more like a punishment than a reward. Instead of feeling satisfied after finishing a major storyline, I was given another repair grind. That completely killed the sense of achievement for me.

I understand this may fit the game's design philosophy, where the journey never truly ends, but players who enjoy games with clear progression and rewarding conclusions may find this frustrating.

What I loved:

Beautiful universe and atmosphere.
Excellent base-building system.
Great freedom to explore.
Amazing visual updates over the years.

What I didn't enjoy:

Main missions often feel like long tutorials.
Too much repetitive travel between objectives.
Story progression feels slow.
The ending of the Atlas path doesn't feel rewarding.
Damaging the player's equipment after a major milestone discourages rather than motivates.

Overall, I respect the incredible work and dedication the developers have put into No Man's Sky over the years. It's simply not the type of progression-focused experience I personally enjoy. I may return in the future if friends want to play together, but as a solo player, I was hoping for a more satisfying sense of accomplishment after completing the main storyline.

its annoying, the game always crash during hyperdrive to other system (because of too much animation, when they could just simplify that loading screen into a static one as an option). It also has several bugs in some mission quests, where they don't complete and had to restart. Once you are warped in a new area, some objects take too long to load, especially on settlement, anomaly, and freighter, the walls and floor are missing, and takes about a minute or two to load the surroundings. Plus the missions are too repetitive that it becomes frustrating especially the "Base Computer Archives" also "Deep Ocean" (you go back and forth with base terminals which feels like a grind, no story but just a log text that you read from the terminal) and "Agricultural Research" (going back and forth from planet base to freighter ship farmer just to plant every species, why not just plant them all together and harvest all at once but no, the developers make you grind those repetitive waypoints). The developers lack creativity in story so they just make you grind going from point A to point B, then to top all your worse experience, the game crash during hyperdrive to another system. So overall, for a game that has been launched since 2016, it does feel like the game is still in beta phase when it should already be fun and engaging to play. Wish it had more better story or maybe adding a family system/ love interest into it. There is no gender selection for your player.

citations.review_text:
Meh

I kept hearing how this is THE game to represent a game studio that flopped on release and then redeemed itself by not letting go and improving on it so much that it became a really good game. It's okay, but doesn't reach the hype. Event mini-boss type enemies often spawn underground, ship gets stuck inside freighters when leaving airlock, mission objective sometimes breaking, and several other issues. In my opinion, it barely hits the "okay" category, not good, not terrible, but I won't be coming back to it. Get it on sale, or pass.

I desperately want to enjoy playing this. I log in from time to time to see if the GAME BREAKING GLITCHES have gotten better. Still no. I just logged in. It spawned me below my corvette. I went up the ramp walked around a corner and got stuck in a wall as I grazed past it. Could not move at all. Mind you my corvette is not complicated. No illegal/mod placements. All standard pieces. less than 1 minute back in and I'm already restarting. Nope. I'm out. You want me to invest time. I want to invest time. but the fricking glitches...

the last time I quit playing out of frustration was an expedition where a glitch caused me to lose ALL my expedition stuff to the main save.

The time before that... the time before that... I remember my first base and me leveling the ground...you all know where this is going. NEVER change the ground around your base. That was a time consuming lesson learned.

STOP ADDING CRAP. FIX YOUR GAME. I BEG YOU.

This game is a lot of kinda cool ideas all mashed together and left half-baked.  
The exploration is impressive in its breadth, but ultimately disappointing in depth.  After a point, everything is pretty 'same old, same old'.
The game is PvE, which is good because it prevents griefing and other abuses, but it does mean starship combat is rather uninteresting.
There are bugs galore that go forever unfixed.  Most annoying are the unsolvable clipping errors and the game forgets changes you make to planetary terrain.
On the plus side, the game is a single purchase, works even on an aging, mid-grade gaming laptop under linux, has an impressively massive open world, and progress isn't agonizingly grindy.
On the minus side, the bugs are persistent, the game world is impressively static (nothing you do matters to any npc faction), very few of the gameplay concepts are fully executed, and, even though you can cross galaxies, you can't secure a load of toxic waste in the bed of a truck.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that multiplayer features and co-op mechanics encounter various bugs and syncing problems.

citations.review_text:
With a very heavy heart I have to leave a negative review for this game.

The game showed so much potential, it definitely has a SOUL, and the creators have a really good eye for details, and it is not a bad game by any means. However, so many core mechanics are flawed that it makes me cry in real life.  I really looked forward to playing this game together with my husband, but that experience turned into a catastrophic failure.

Base Building: You cannot build a base together because the base computer is personalized. You can't even place them side by side. Terrain in multiplayer bugs horribly. What you remove using the terraforming tool comes back; what you add disappears. Buildings sink, and NPCs clip through the floor.
Spaceships & Capital Ships: You cannot build your spaceship together. You can't even invite your friend to your capital ship, as they get placed into a completely different instance. You cannot even properly see your friend's ship name.
The "Co-op" Corvette: The only spaceship designed to fly together (the corvette) does not work properly in multiplayer. The mission board does not properly sync between you and your friend, you can get teleported out of the ship if you stand in the wrong spot, and you are not allowed to add parts to help your friend build it. Many other minor glitches on top of those.
Broken Quests: Many quests are impossible to complete if you are in someone else's game. NPCs who talked to your friend will no longer talk to you, and destination markers bug out and lead to nowhere.

This game is absolutely not for completionists or people who love collecting in-game items:
FOMO / Past Content: Most of the coolest stuff you encounter or have seen in trailers (including spaceships) you will never ever get. They come from past expeditions that are over, and today there is no way to complete them.
Your collection inventory is strictly limited. You have  N amount of spaceships you can own and save, N amount of weapons, an N amount of pe…

THE GOOD:
Very fun, relaxing game. It kinda feels like Minecraft in space in the sense that there is A LOT of stuff to do, but there's not too much forcing the player to do it and also all that stuff that you can do is not all that complex, just grindy, but I like the grind! It's a cool loop to traverse the galaxy and explore different worlds.

I like how you have to interact with a specific race in order to gain reputation and learn their language, again, grindy but actually rewarding because you see the rewards in literally being able to sorta understand the guys after a while.

When you actually find the right planet, the right place where the sun shines just right. The game looks great from then on. Even better when you find that moment again, 20 solar systems later.

The music is nice I guess, sometimes it fits really nicely but sometimes its a biiiit too much...

Base building is cool, resource gathering is cool, I like industrializing hellish planets lol

I like the nanite upgrade systems, the feeling of reaching your characters potential movement and damage capacities is nice. Scanner upgrade go BRRRRRRR

In general, I would say is a very immersive game, I truly feel like a space traveler when I play No Man's Sky, and I see that as a huge achievement for the game, the movement of the spaceship feels nice most of the time, using the pulse drive and finding stuff in deep space is just cool man.

THE BAD:
THERES SO MANY BUGS MAN
Multiplayer can easily become a very frustrating experience with the bugs, infinite enemy waves, immortal bosses, canceled drops... It happens often, which encourages players/friends to play apart from one another, even more so in combats, which SHOULD be very fun as a team. Speaking about combat...

All ground fights are a joke. The only way to make a ground battle remotely challenging is to fight in an infernal world, surrounded by mountains, in the middle of a storm. And still, fighting is just kinda transactional.…

citations.review_text: This is a beautiful game.  As an artist, I feel like I'm navigating a work of visual art on most planets.  Not only is it beautiful, but it is the space game I wanted when I was a child.  You can get in a ship, and actually fly out into space, fly to another planet, and land with no cutscenes or load screens.  The game is filled with creative sci-fi props and fun things to do.  Building, fishing, smuggling, fighting, mining, and running settlements are just a few of the things you can engage with in the game.  The races are really interesting as well.  The only cons are that some of the games mechanics can be a little shallow, combat isn't very difficult, and it might be a little too easy to get rich.  Over all, an enormous, fun, creative, and beautiful game.  I've really enjoyed it.  It's one of those games I keep coming back to like minecraft.

No Man's Sky has long been one of my favorite games. It's a space exploration, survival game, where you start off on a single planet filled with beautiful sights given the simple task of repairing your starship, only to find you're only on one of the many stunning planets in your star system, and that system is also one of the infinitely-many systems in the game.

You get to explore, see new planets, new star-system types, spend tens to hundreds of hours doing just that because really it's hard to run out of new things to see, or you can explore these worlds and look for your quintessential starship, mine resources and earn enough money to get the upgrades you want for it to make it perfect, upgrade it and make it better, etc.
And once you're done with your starship, there are still a plethora of things to do. You can do the same thing with your multi-tool, which is the thing that allows you to mine, fish, and do combat - yes there's combat in the game too - in the game. 
Once you're done with that, you could go and interact with the other lifeforms and yes they exist too. You could start learning their language and finally be able to understand them, or make your relationship with their race better by doing quests for them or giving them gifts... and even then you're far from finished.
There's a solid base building system in the game as well, so you can build your own very base/home too, potentially after spending many hours finding the perfect planet to build it on.
Done that? Well I forgot to talk about just how cool each of these worlds could be. There are many different species of animals and many many different plants and minerals on each of these wonderful planets. Each of them also has a unique atmosphere, weather, climate and ecosystem, and a different set of hazardous things too. You could then find some ocean worlds and get to see and explore an underwater world as well...

I can't possibly name every thing there is in the game. There's just so mu…

No Man's Sky is a gem of gaming for anyone who likes sandbox games and exploration.
While on launch it was known as one of the biggest disappointments in gaming history, it has come a long way and redeemed itself in the eyes of many. 

The gameplay loop is fun and engaging, while ground combat is nothing special, the ship combat, resource gathering and exploration are all quite enjoyable. The graphics are nice looking with its own art style that is pleasant to look at. Exploration always yields something tangible and useful to you not just pretty vistas. The community is one of the best in the gaming space, just all around incredible people. 

For those looking for exploration and getting overwhelmed by all the things to see and do in a vast space game, I believe it's the perfect fit.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the universe exploration and procedural generation as eventually feeling repetitive or shallow after extended playtime.

citations.review_text: Very broad and very shallow. Only interesting as long as you're finding new mechanics to explore and it might take a while to find most of it. Every new mechanic, however, reveals itself to be paper thin quite quickly, leading every brief excitement of finding something new once every few hours to end inf a flat note mere minutes afterwards.

First 100 hours made me feel like this game was too good to be true. It looks incredible and the amount of features and random things you can do here is honestly quite insane. The problem is, however, that once you get your dream corvette and a freighter you start noticing that that the universe isn't really as deep as you thought at the beginning.

My overall impression is that this game is really good at creating the illusion of being free in a massive universe, but about 100 hours is enough for you to realize the game is still pretty shallow. But to be honest, there's no game out there that runs this well and allows you to have so much freedom and the update cadence is absolutely stellar.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that time-gated expeditions prevent returning or new players from acquiring past rewards and recipes.

citations.review_text: Time gated expeditions means if you miss them, you’ll never get the recipes from them. So if you’re thinking of picking up this game after a few years, you won’t get some of the content.

Nice and chill. Mechanics are simple and the gameplay loop is kind of whatever you want it to be. Gameplay loop at its core revolves arounds gathering minerals from different planets and traveling between systems inhabited by either small, trade oriented lizard merchants who do not seem entirely trustworthy, orcs with a very warrior-like mentality who sound like they might invade a neighbour if given a chance or clankers. There looks to be a 4th race but I'm not at the station to socialize so read a wiki or something.

Expeditions bring a new twist typically revolving around the latest update, some have been great, others not so much. A bit of variety is always welcome regardless. Most important part is that the game has taken galactic steps forward from the abomination it used to be. Try it out, at this point the content is so varied there is bound to be something there for almost anyone. I've spent a bit of time with this game and still haven't tried everything the game has to offer.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the core gameplay loop as centering on resource gathering, exploration, base building, and upgrading equipment across procedurally generated planets.

citations.review_text: This is a beautiful game.  As an artist, I feel like I'm navigating a work of visual art on most planets.  Not only is it beautiful, but it is the space game I wanted when I was a child.  You can get in a ship, and actually fly out into space, fly to another planet, and land with no cutscenes or load screens.  The game is filled with creative sci-fi props and fun things to do.  Building, fishing, smuggling, fighting, mining, and running settlements are just a few of the things you can engage with in the game.  The races are really interesting as well.  The only cons are that some of the games mechanics can be a little shallow, combat isn't very difficult, and it might be a little too easy to get rich.  Over all, an enormous, fun, creative, and beautiful game.  I've really enjoyed it.  It's one of those games I keep coming back to like minecraft.

No Man's Sky has long been one of my favorite games. It's a space exploration, survival game, where you start off on a single planet filled with beautiful sights given the simple task of repairing your starship, only to find you're only on one of the many stunning planets in your star system, and that system is also one of the infinitely-many systems in the game.

You get to explore, see new planets, new star-system types, spend tens to hundreds of hours doing just that because really it's hard to run out of new things to see, or you can explore these worlds and look for your quintessential starship, mine resources and earn enough money to get the upgrades you want for it to make it perfect, upgrade it and make it better, etc.
And once you're done with your starship, there are still a plethora of things to do. You can do the same thing with your multi-tool, which is the thing that allows you to mine, fish, and do combat - yes there's combat in the game too - in the game. 
Once you're done with that, you could go and interact with the other lifeforms and yes they exist too. You could start learning their language and finally be able to understand them, or make your relationship with their race better by doing quests for them or giving them gifts... and even then you're far from finished.
There's a solid base building system in the game as well, so you can build your own very base/home too, potentially after spending many hours finding the perfect planet to build it on.
Done that? Well I forgot to talk about just how cool each of these worlds could be. There are many different species of animals and many many different plants and minerals on each of these wonderful planets. Each of them also has a unique atmosphere, weather, climate and ecosystem, and a different set of hazardous things too. You could then find some ocean worlds and get to see and explore an underwater world as well...

I can't possibly name every thing there is in the game. There's just so mu…

Love the game, it always gives me a sense of awe and exploration. But that feeling dies very quickly when you realize how empty this world really is....

There's a lot to do in the game now compared to what you could do in the past, but the game still just trickles down to:
- warp to new system
- find and collect resources
- maybe check the space station if you are still getting unlocks
- build base/ship/upgrade

there's side stuff to do, but generally, that's the loop.

I never feel like i find cool ruins and explore... maybe an independant large city.. or any form of curated content..

The whole world just feels like it was built for me to take over.. every overseers of a settlement bends over and lets you take over the settlement instantly.. any freighter you get on will instantly go "oh great warrior! i am beneath you! would you like to become the captain of this vessel?"... 

and hey.. that it's the point, i guess... this is a simulation that you are in and the simulation is built for you, the interloper... it just feels so empty and dead...........

No Man's Sky is awesome until, quite suddenly, it is not.  You begin by awakening on an unknown planet with a likely hostile environment (maybe), and you'll have to repair your equipment and survive using only what is available around you.  Over a few hours, you'll discover new elements and new recipes to build a base and repair your ship while discovering more about the game's world.  

Over a few more hours, No Man's Sky abandons the Open World Survival Model and morphs into an exploration game.  You'll have to find and explore many different planets and biomes to discover the big mystery behind who you are and why you are here, as well as learn the languages of the many (three) races that populate the galaxy and have surprisingly little to say or offer.  You will not need to survive on any of these planets.  We are done with that now.  

Of course, that doesn't mean you're scot-free.  No, there is a thriving economy and you can learn to master it.  Make billions by discovering and running trade routes between systems to maximize profit.  Learn the secrets of the trade radar.  Or you can discover recipes to create your own products and run factories to also make billions of credits.  Billions!  You'll need to upgrade your ship's warp drive to get to the planets with the most valuable ore and flora, of course, so get ready to spend!  Until you've bought everything.  Then you'll never need money ever again. Ever.  

Worried about this new venture cutting into your exploration time?  Don't be.  Exploring is completely unnecessary and can be fully wrapped up in less than 20 hours along side the main quest, as planets begin to repeat themselves down to even minor details very quickly.

There is a fantastic main story that deals in the themes of life, free will, the nature of existence.  Enjoy it, because once it is over, it is never addressed again outside of another repeatable questline masquerading as content.  Content that adds nothing but repeats of the same conten…

claims.claim: Reviewers point out that despite a wide variety of activities and planets, individual mechanics and planetary structures can feel repetitive and shallow after extended playtime.

citations.review_text: Would recommend with a heavy asterisk - *The game is as wide as an ocean but as deep as a puddle. The first time you interact with a new mechanic/event/update content it's interesting but you'll find that it won't keep your attention after you go through the very few variations in each form of content. The game is very pretty and can be fun if you have a friend interested in building a cool base with you but if you're looking for genuine challenge or payoff you're probably not getting it here.

Very broad and very shallow. Only interesting as long as you're finding new mechanics to explore and it might take a while to find most of it. Every new mechanic, however, reveals itself to be paper thin quite quickly, leading every brief excitement of finding something new once every few hours to end inf a flat note mere minutes afterwards.

First 100 hours made me feel like this game was too good to be true. It looks incredible and the amount of features and random things you can do here is honestly quite insane. The problem is, however, that once you get your dream corvette and a freighter you start noticing that that the universe isn't really as deep as you thought at the beginning.

My overall impression is that this game is really good at creating the illusion of being free in a massive universe, but about 100 hours is enough for you to realize the game is still pretty shallow. But to be honest, there's no game out there that runs this well and allows you to have so much freedom and the update cadence is absolutely stellar.

Sadly for all of the years of development and work, the game is still boring. Tons of updates brought a lot of new and different things to do, but every old and new mechanic is simple and lacks progression. The worst part is that with the size of the galaxy - your experience, except visually, does not change. If you fought sentinels on this planet it will be same experience 100 star systems away. Same old few missions, same old buildings on different edges of a galaxy. It's dull in it's samyness. 
Exploration doesn't matter, mechanically planets have same missions, same underlying structure, you don't need to prepare or care on what planet you are, except what resources you need. And very fast it becomes logistics and resource management game instead of a exploration game. Which wouldn't be a problem if resource management and logistics wouldn't be so shallow and boring.
Trade doesn't matter, interaction between factions is none existent and it makes every star system samish and non-important. Space fights are dull. What type of space ship you fly doesn't really matter, partly because of uninspired mechanics, partly because there is no real difference between said space ships. Of course, except visually and how much stuff it can carry.
In the end you're just watching how much more stuff you have, more currencies, more bases, more pretty ships, more resources, but in the end you're doing the same thing that you did in the star system you spawned. And if you don't enjoy this bare bones game loop, it depressingly wouldn't change in 100s of star systems.
I would like to love this game, but sadly after all the years of development, it's - ironically, for all of it's visual diversity, bare bones, knee deep and generic in gameplay.

This game is a lot of kinda cool ideas all mashed together and left half-baked.  
The exploration is impressive in its breadth, but ultimately disappointing in depth.  After a point, everything is pretty 'same old, same old'.
The game is PvE, which is good because it prevents griefing and other abuses, but it does mean starship combat is rather uninteresting.
There are bugs galore that go forever unfixed.  Most annoying are the unsolvable clipping errors and the game forgets changes you make to planetary terrain.
On the plus side, the game is a single purchase, works even on an aging, mid-grade gaming laptop under linux, has an impressively massive open world, and progress isn't agonizingly grindy.
On the minus side, the bugs are persistent, the game world is impressively static (nothing you do matters to any npc faction), very few of the gameplay concepts are fully executed, and, even though you can cross galaxies, you can't secure a load of toxic waste in the bed of a truck.
